title: Emerson's Compensation
hookLine: every act rewards or punishes itself, Emerson believed (Compensation)

cards: Near the start of the essay, Emerson describes a sermon he disagreed with.

He says he heard a preacher explain that in this world things are unjust: the wicked do well, the good suffer, and the balance will be set right later, in the life to come. It's a serious view, with deep roots.
Emerson didn't argue about the life to come. What bothered him was the picture of this life, the idea that cheating actually pays here and now, and only gets corrected afterward.
His essay answers that the books are balanced sooner than that. He called it Compensation.

teach.b: First, the big claim, in four words: "Every act rewards itself." Not later. In the act.
A deed, as Emerson sees it, carries its own result inside it.
Second, his picture from nature: pairs everywhere. Light and dark, heat and cold, the tide coming in and going out, breathing in and breathing out.
Nothing in nature, he says, comes without its opposite; a gain somewhere means a cost somewhere else. He thought human life worked the same way. Third, the hard line.
"Crime and punishment grow out of one stem." The lie and the fear of being found out sprout together. The cheat gets the money and also gets to be a person who cheats, and has to live inside that.
The good act works the same way: the kindness is already doing its work in the one who gave it. Emerson borrows an old Greek saying for this: "The dice of God are always loaded."
The game isn't random; it's rigged toward balance. Fourth, the honest limit. Emerson can make this sound too neat, as if every life comes out even.
Some suffering doesn't look balanced at all.
So hold Compensation as a lens, not a guarantee.

teach.h: THE DICE OF GOD ARE ALWAYS LOADED.
teach.b: Some results show up fast, some take years, and some you'll have to take on trust. Still, sometimes the first person an act changes is the one who did it.

how: Some readers use Emerson's Compensation as a lens for noticing how their actions shape them from the inside, while keeping in mind that he can make life sound more evenly balanced than it is.

games.q: you're Emerson in the pew. the preacher says the wicked prosper now and the good are repaid later. what do you do?
o: nod along; it's the usual view.
answer it with an essay: the books balance sooner.
stand up and argue about the life to come.
games.why: he wrote Compensation, leaving the life to come alone, and arguing that every act rewards itself here and now.

practice: Bring back something small you did in the last day or two, a short temper, a favor done unasked, a corner cut, a promise kept, and without judging it, follow it forward.
What happened next, inside you or between you and someone else, and how did it leave you feeling about yourself? Watch the result grow out of the act, like a plant from its seed.

carryVoice: Your line: it comes back. Light and dark, the tide in and out: nothing comes alone. Until tomorrow.
